title: In heap-dump analysis, what is the difference between shallow heap and retained heap, and why do you sort by retained heap to find memory accumulators?
shortTitle: What is shallow heap vs retained heap in heap dump analysis?

s1_definition.profdef: In heap-dump analysis, shallow heap is the memory occupied by a single object itself, counting only its own fields and object header, not the objects it refers to. Retained heap is the total memory that would be freed if that object were garbage collected, which is the object's own shallow size plus the shallow sizes of all objects that are reachable only through it and would therefore also become garbage. You sort by retained heap, not shallow heap, because retained heap reveals which object is truly holding the most memory alive, whereas shallow heap can make a small object that pins a huge subgraph look insignificant.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh's manager at National Bank of India holds a single key. The key itself is tiny, that is its shallow size. But that one key is the only thing that unlocks a giant vault full of folders, and if you take the key away, the whole vault's contents can be cleared out. The retained size is the key plus everything in that vault that nothing else can reach. If you judged importance by the size of the key alone, you would ignore the person responsible for an entire vault. That is why, when hunting a memory problem, you look at retained size, because it tells you who is actually keeping all that memory alive.
s1_definition.oneliner: Shallow heap is an object's own size; retained heap is everything that would be freed if it were collected, so you sort by retained heap to find the true memory accumulator rather than a small object that secretly anchors a huge subgraph.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In heap-dump analysis, shallow heap is the memory occupied by a single object itself, counting only its own fields and object header, not the objects it refers to. Retained heap is the total memory that would be freed if that object were garbage collected, which is the object's own shallow size plus the shallow sizes of all objects that are reachable only through it and would therefore also become garbage. You sort by retained heap, not shallow heap, because retained heap reveals which object is truly holding the most memory alive, whereas shallow heap can make a small object that pins a huge subgraph look insignificant.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh's manager at National Bank of India holds a single key. The key itself is tiny, that is its shallow size. But that one key is the only thing that unlocks a giant vault full of folders, and if you take the key away, the whole vault's contents can be cleared out. The retained size is the key plus everything in that vault that nothing else can reach. If you judged importance by the size of the key alone, you would ignore the person responsible for an entire vault. That is why, when hunting a memory problem, you look at retained size, because it tells you who is actually keeping all that memory alive.

**One line to remember:** Shallow heap is an object's own size; retained heap is everything that would be freed if it were collected, so you sort by retained heap to find the true memory accumulator rather than a small object that secretly anchors a huge subgraph.

sections.s2_technical:
Every object occupies some memory for its own header and its own fields; that is its shallow heap. For a HashMap object, the shallow heap is small, essentially a handful of fields like the table reference, the size, and the load factor, because the map object itself does not contain the entries, it only references them. Shallow heap is useful for understanding per-instance cost, but on its own it is misleading when you are hunting a leak, because the biggest consumers are rarely large single objects; they are usually small objects that reference enormous graphs.

Retained heap captures that graph. The retained set of an object is the set of objects that would be removed by the garbage collector if that object became unreachable, meaning the object itself plus everything reachable only through it. The retained heap is the total shallow size of that retained set. For the same HashMap, the retained heap includes the internal table array, every Node, and every key and value that nothing outside the map still references, which could be hundreds of megabytes. So the map's shallow heap might be forty bytes while its retained heap is two hundred megabytes. This is why retained heap is the number that matters for finding what is actually consuming memory.

The reason you sort by retained heap when analyzing a dump is to find the dominator, the single object whose removal would free the most memory. Tools build a dominator tree, where object A dominates object B if every path from the garbage-collection roots to B passes through A; A's retained heap is then the sum over everything it dominates. Sorting the dominator tree by retained heap puts the biggest accumulator at the top. In a banking leak, this is typically a long-lived singleton, such as a Spring-managed cache bean, holding an unbounded Map or List; its shallow size is tiny but its retained heap is the whole leaked collection. A concrete signature is a single CacheService instance with a retained heap of hundreds of megabytes, which immediately tells you the cache is unbounded.

A few nuances matter at a senior level. Shared objects complicate retained size: if two objects both reference the same string, that string is not counted in either one's retained set because removing one object alone would not free it; it only appears in the retained set of their common dominator. This is why the dominator tree, rather than naive reachability, gives a correct and non-double-counted retained size. Also, the difference between shallow and retained is exactly why you should never diagnose a leak by instance count or shallow size alone; a million tiny Node objects might each have a trivial shallow size, but their common dominator, the map, has a massive retained size that points you to the real culprit. The practical rule I follow is: open the dominator tree, sort by retained heap, and the object at the top is almost always either the leak itself or one reference away from it.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's fraud-scoring service slowly consumed memory until it crashed. A junior engineer looked at the heap and saw millions of small transaction-record objects and concluded the records were the problem, but each record's shallow size was tiny. This is exactly the shallow-versus-retained distinction, because the records were only symptoms; something was retaining them.

Problem 2 — Sorting by retained heap instead revealed a single scoring-cache object with a retained heap of hundreds of megabytes, because it held an unbounded map of every transaction ever scored. This is exactly why you sort by retained heap, because it pointed straight at the one small object that was anchoring the entire leaked graph.

In the mini-project we build a `ScoringCache` that retains transaction records in an unbounded map, allocate many records, and compute an approximate shallow-versus-retained comparison using instrumentation-style sizing logic in plain code, logging how a tiny cache object retains a huge graph. The lesson is to look at retained, not shallow.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the demo
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/retained/RetainedHeapDemo.java

# Run and, to inspect for real, dump the heap on OOM and open it in Eclipse MAT
java -Xms512m -Xmx512m \
     -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=./heapdump.hprof \
     -cp out com.bank.retained.RetainedHeapDemo

# In Eclipse MAT: open the dominator tree, sort by Retained Heap →
# ScoringCache sits at the top despite a tiny shallow size.
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one ScoringCache object and five hundred thousand transaction records fed into it.

Step 1: The single ScoringCache is created. Its own shallow size is tiny, just a header and a reference to its internal map.

Step 2: Five hundred thousand records are scored. Each `score` call creates a TransactionRecord with a two-hundred-fifty-six-byte payload and puts it in the cache's map, which never evicts. Each record's shallow size is modest.

Step 3: The demo computes the two perspectives. Shallow heap of the cache is around twenty-four bytes, which, looked at alone, makes the cache seem harmless.

Step 4: Retained heap of the cache is the cache plus every record reachable only through it plus the map's internal nodes, which sums to well over one hundred megabytes. This is the number that reveals the real consumer.

Step 5: The logs make the point: sorting a heap dump by retained heap would place this tiny cache at the very top, immediately identifying it as the accumulator, and the fix is to bound the cache so its retained heap stays small.

```text
[INFO] cache SHALLOW heap ≈ 24 bytes (tiny!)
[INFO] cache RETAINED heap ≈ 157 MB (500000 records held alive)
[WARNING] Sort a heap dump by RETAINED heap → this tiny cache is the top accumulator
[INFO] Fix: bound the cache (LRU/size/TTL) so retained heap stays small
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  GC Roots
    │
    ▼
  ScoringCache (shallow ≈ 24 bytes)   ← dominator of the whole subgraph
    │ cache map ref
    ▼
  HashMap (shallow ≈ 48 bytes)
    │ table[]
    ▼
  [ Node → Node → Node ... ×500,000 ]
         │ each value
         ▼
      TransactionRecord (shallow ≈ 296 bytes each)
         │ payload
         ▼
      byte[256]

  SHALLOW(ScoringCache) = 24 bytes       ← looks harmless
  RETAINED(ScoringCache) = everything    ← ~157 MB (the real leak)
    reachable ONLY through it

  Sort dominator tree by RETAINED → ScoringCache at the TOP.
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Shallow vs Retained Heap ═══

  ┌─ Definitions ─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Shallow heap  : object's own header + fields only      │
  │ Retained heap : shallow of the object + shallow of all  │
  │                 objects reachable ONLY through it       │
  │                 (= what GC frees if it dies)            │
  │ Dominator     : A dominates B if every GC-root→B path   │
  │                 goes through A; retained = sum dominated │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ScoringCache (retainer)
    shallow  = 24 B            ← per-instance cost
    retained = 24 B + Σ(nodes + records + payloads) ≈ 157 MB

  Shared-object nuance:
    object referenced by TWO owners → counted only in their
    common dominator's retained set (no double counting)

  Rule: diagnose leaks by RETAINED heap in the dominator tree,
        NOT by instance count or shallow size.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
In heap-dump analysis there are two sizes for every object, and knowing the difference is the whole game when hunting a leak. Shallow heap is the memory an object occupies by itself, counting only its own object header and its own fields, and crucially not the objects it refers to. For a HashMap, the shallow heap is tiny, just a few fields like the table reference, the size, and the load factor, because the map object does not physically contain its entries, it only points at them. Retained heap is completely different: it is the total memory that would actually be freed if that object were garbage collected, which is the object's own shallow size plus the shallow sizes of every object that is reachable only through it and would therefore also become garbage.

The reason I always sort by retained heap, never shallow heap, is that the biggest memory consumers are rarely large single objects. They are usually small objects that anchor enormous graphs. That same HashMap might have a shallow size of forty bytes but a retained heap of two hundred megabytes, because its retained set includes the internal table array, every node, and every key and value that nothing outside the map still references. If I judged importance by shallow size, I would completely overlook the object that is actually holding all that memory alive.

Tools formalize this with the dominator tree. One object dominates another when every path from the garbage-collection roots to that other object passes through it, and an object's retained heap is the sum of everything it dominates. Sorting the dominator tree by retained heap puts the true accumulator at the top. In my banking experience this is almost always a long-lived singleton, like a Spring-managed cache bean, holding an unbounded map or list; its shallow size is trivial but its retained heap is the entire leaked collection. On a fraud-scoring service I chased, the heap showed millions of tiny transaction records, and a junior engineer blamed the records, but each record's shallow size was negligible. Sorting by retained heap instead pointed immediately at a single scoring-cache object with a retained heap of hundreds of megabytes, because it held an unbounded map of every transaction ever scored.

The senior nuance I add is about shared objects and double counting. If two objects both reference the same string, that string is not counted in either one's retained set, because removing just one of them would not free the string; it only appears in the retained set of their common dominator. That is exactly why the dominator tree, rather than naive reachability, gives a correct retained size without double counting. So my practical rule is simple: open the dominator tree, sort by retained heap, and the object at the top is almost always either the leak itself or one reference away from it, and in a banking service the fix is usually to bound that cache with an eviction policy so its retained heap can never grow without limit.

---

keyPoints: Shallow heap: memory consumed by the object itself (fields only)
Retained heap: memory freed if this object AND everything it exclusively holds is GC-ed
Retained heap reveals the true cost of an object including its dependency tree
Always sort by retained heap to find leak suspects
Eclipse MAT dominator tree shows retained heap per object
